lessons.subject: English literature
lessons.title: Romeo and Juliet: the prologue
lessons.summary: Find out what the opening of Shakespeare's play tells the audience.
lessons.curriculum: Key stage 3 English: reading 2 plays by Shakespeare
pages: Romeo and Juliet opens with a prologue, spoken by the Chorus. It is a sonnet: a poem of 14 lines.
It introduces 2 families in Verona who hate each other: “Two households, both alike in dignity”.
It calls Romeo and Juliet “a pair of star-cross'd lovers” and tells us they will die.
The audience knows the ending from the start, but the characters do not. This creates dramatic irony throughout the play.

check.question: What kind of poem is the prologue?
check.explanation: The prologue is a sonnet: 14 lines that rhyme in a set pattern.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Pythagoras' theorem
lessons.summary: Find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
lessons.curriculum: Key stage 3 maths: use Pythagoras' theorem to solve problems involving right-angled triangles
pages: Pythagoras' theorem works for right-angled triangles. The longest side, opposite the right angle, is called the hypotenuse.
If the shorter sides are a and b, and the hypotenuse is c, then a² + b² = c².
For example, if a = 3 and b = 4, then c² = 9 + 16 = 25. So c = √25 = 5.

check.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 6 centimetres and 8 centimetres. How long is the hypotenuse?

lessons.subject: Science (physics)
lessons.title: Speed
lessons.summary: Work out how fast something moves from distance and time.
lessons.curriculum: Key stage 3 physics: the relationship between average speed, distance and time (speed = distance ÷ time)
pages: Speed tells you how far something travels in a certain time.
Speed = distance ÷ time. With distance in metres and time in seconds, speed is in metres per second (m/s).
A runner covers 100 metres in 20 seconds. Their speed is 100 ÷ 20 = 5m/s.

check.question: A cyclist travels 150 metres in 30 seconds. What is their average speed?

lessons.subject: History
lessons.title: The First World War
lessons.summary: Find out how the war started in 1914 and what fighting was like.
lessons.curriculum: Key stage 3 history: challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world from 1901 to the present day, such as the First World War
pages: On 28 June 1914, Gavrilo Princip shot dead Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo.
Alliances between countries turned this into a wider war. Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914.
On the Western Front, soldiers fought from trenches. On the first day of the Battle of the Somme, 1 July 1916, the British Army had about 57,000 casualties.
Fighting stopped at 11am on 11 November 1918. Every year, people in the UK remember those who died on Armistice Day and Remembrance Sunday.

check.question: When did fighting stop in the First World War?
check.explanation: Fighting stopped with the armistice at 11am on 11 November 1918.
